title: Literals, Parameters, and Constants
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of literals, parameters, and constants.
Apply numeric literals in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn literals, parameters, and constants through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Literals, Parameters, and Constants matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of literals, parameters, and constants is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Numeric literals, String literals, Date and time literals, Boolean literals. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Numeric literals
items.text: Numeric literals works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: String literals
items.text: String literals depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Date and time literals
items.text: Date and time literals needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Boolean literals
items.text: Boolean literals works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Positional and named parameter concepts
items.text: Positional and named parameter concepts should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

items.title: Literal values vs. query parameters
items.text: Literal values vs. query parameters should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.code: SELECT 42::integer AS item_count, 19.95::numeric(8,2) AS unit_price, DATE '2026-01-10' AS sample_date, TRUE AS is_active;
content_blocks.expected_output: The result returns explicitly typed numeric, date, and Boolean values. The :: cast syntax is PostgreSQL-specific; CAST(value AS type) is the standard-style alternative.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate literals, parameters, and constants using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic numeric literals and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Literals, Parameters, and Constants is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
